claim: During meiosis homologous chromosomes undergo crossover recombination.
source: During meiosis homologous chromosomes undergo crossover recombination.
evidence: This is a fundamental statement about meiosis that is part of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Sequence differences between homologs can locally inhibit crossovers.
source: Sequence differences between homologs can locally inhibit crossovers.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript to previous work.

claim: Nucleotide diversity and population-scaled recombination are positively correlated in eukaryote genomes.
source: Despite this, nucleotide diversity and population-scaled recombination are positively correlated in eukaryote genomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and is a known observation in population genetics.

claim: Hybrids of Arabidopsis lines crossed to 32 diverse accessions showed significantly higher and lower crossovers than homozygotes.
source: To investigate interactions between heterozygosity and recombination we crossed Arabidopsis lines carrying fluorescent crossover reporters to 32 diverse accessions and observed hybrids with significantly higher and lower crossovers than homozygotes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Heterozygous regions increase crossovers when juxtaposed with homozygous regions.
source: Using recombinant populations derived from these crosses we observed that heterozygous regions increase crossovers when juxtaposed with homozygous regions, which reciprocally decrease.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from recombinant populations.

claim: Homozygous regions reciprocally decrease crossovers when juxtaposed with heterozygous regions.
source: Using recombinant populations derived from these crosses we observed that heterozygous regions increase crossovers when juxtaposed with homozygous regions, which reciprocally decrease.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from recombinant populations.

claim: Total crossovers measured by chiasmata were unchanged when heterozygosity was varied.
source: Total crossovers measured by chiasmata were unchanged when heterozygosity was varied, consistent with homeostatic control.
evidence: This is supported by cytological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Crossover remodeling at homozygosity-heterozygosity junctions requires interference.
source: Crossover remodeling at homozygosity-heterozygosity junctions requires interference, and non-interfering repair is inefficient in heterozygous regions.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using mutants with altered crossover pathways.

claim: Non-interfering repair is inefficient in heterozygous regions.
source: Crossover remodeling at homozygosity-heterozygosity junctions requires interference, and non-interfering repair is inefficient in heterozygous regions.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using mutants with altered crossover pathways.

claim: Heterozygous regions show stronger crossover interference.
source: As a consequence, heterozygous regions show stronger crossover interference.
evidence: This is supported by interference measurements in the manuscript.

claim: Sexual reproduction via meiosis is highly conserved within eukaryotes.
source: Sexual reproduction via meiosis is highly conserved within eukaryotes and allows recombination of genetic variation within populations (Barton and Charlesworth, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: Meiosis allows recombination of genetic variation within populations.
source: Sexual reproduction via meiosis is highly conserved within eukaryotes and allows recombination of genetic variation within populations (Barton and Charlesworth, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: Meiotic crossovers form via the repair of DNA double-strand breaks generated by the SPO11 endonuclease.
source: Meiotic crossovers form via the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) generated by the SPO11 endonuclease (Bergerat et al., 1997; Keeney et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: Nucleolytic resection of DSBs generates 3′ single-stranded DNA which is bound by the RAD51 and DMC1 recombinases.
source: Nucleolytic resection of DSBs generates 3′ single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), which is bound by the RAD51 and DMC1 recombinases (Bishop et al., 1992; Shinohara et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: Chiasmata hold chromosomes together and ensure that homologous pairs segregate to opposite cell poles.
source: Chiasmata hold chromosomes together and ensure that homologous pairs segregate to opposite cell poles, so that gametes inherit a balanced chromosome number (Page and Hawley, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: Many eukaryote species experience 1–2 crossovers per chromosome despite large variation in genome size.
source: Crossover numbers are under tight control, with many eukaryote species experiencing 1–2 per chromosome, despite large variation in genome size (Villeneuve and Hillers, 2001; Smukowski and Noor, 2011; Henderson, 2012; Mercier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Arabidopsis approximately 200 DSBs form per meiosis.
source: In Arabidopsis ∼200 DSBs form per meiosis and proceed to form strand invasion intermediates, of which ∼10 are repaired as crossovers, with the excess being repaired as non-crossovers, or via intersister recombination (Giraut et al., 2011; Ferdous et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012; Drouaud et al., 2013; Wijnker et al., 2013; Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Approximately 10 DSBs are repaired as crossovers in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis ∼200 DSBs form per meiosis and proceed to form strand invasion intermediates, of which ∼10 are repaired as crossovers, with the excess being repaired as non-crossovers, or via intersister recombination (Giraut et al., 2011; Ferdous et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012; Drouaud et al., 2013; Wijnker et al., 2013; Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 80–85% of wild type crossovers are dependent on the ZMM pathway and show interference.
source: 80–85% of wild type crossovers are dependent on the ZMM pathway (MSH4, MSH5, MER3, HEI10, ZIP4, SHOC1, PTD) and show interference, that is, they are spaced further apart than expected at random (Copenhaver et al., 2002; Higgins et al., 2004, 2008a; Chen et al., 2005; Mercier et al., 2005; Chelysheva et al., 2007, 2010, 2012; Macaisne et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The minority of crossovers are non-interfering and require MUS81.
source: The remaining minority of crossovers are non-interfering and require MUS81 (Berchowitz et al., 2007; Higgins et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chiasmata are still observed in msh4 mus81 double mutants, indicating additional crossover pathways exist.
source: However, as chiasmata are still observed in msh4 mus81 double mutants, additional crossover pathways must exist (Higgins et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and logical inference.

claim: The majority of interhomolog strand invasion intermediates are dissolved by the FANCM helicase.
source: The majority of interhomolog strand invasion intermediates are dissolved by the FANCM helicase, which acts with the MHF1 and MHF2 co-factors (Crismani et al., 2012; Knoll et al., 2012; Girard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mutations in FANCM, MHF1 and MHF2 cause dramatic increases in non-interfering crossovers.
source: Mutations in FANCM, MHF1 and MHF2 cause dramatic increases in non-interfering crossovers (Crismani et al., 2012; Knoll et al., 2012; Girard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Insertion-deletion and single nucleotide polymorphisms suppress crossovers at the scale of hotspots (kb) in fungi, plants and mammals.
source: For example, insertion-deletion (indel) and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) suppress crossovers at the scale of hotspots (kb) in fungi, plants and mammals (Dooner, 1986; Borts and Haber, 1987; Jeffreys and Neumann, 2005; Baudat and de Massy, 2007; Cole et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Heteroduplex base-pair mismatches inhibit recombination following interhomolog strand invasion.
source: This is thought to occur due to heteroduplex base-pair mismatches inhibiting recombination, following interhomolog strand invasion.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenomenon.

claim: Large scale chromosome rearrangements, such as inversions or translocations, suppress crossovers.
source: Large scale chromosome rearrangements, such as inversions or translocations, also suppress crossovers (Schwander et al., 2014; Thompson and Jiggins, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Linkage disequilibrium-based crossover estimates and sequence diversity (π) are positively correlated in Arabidopsis at varying physical scales.
source: For example, linkage disequilibrium-based crossover estimates and sequence diversity (π) are positively correlated in Arabidopsis at varying physical scales (Figure 1A and Table 1) (Cao et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data presented in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: Positive or negative directional selection can reduce diversity at linked sites, with a greater effect in regions of low recombination.
source: For example, positive or negative directional selection can reduce diversity at linked sites, with a greater effect in regions of low recombination, known as hitchhiking and background selection (Hill and Robertson, 1966; Hudson and Kaplan, 1995; Nordborg et al., 1996; Smith and Haigh, 2007; Cutter and Payseur, 2013; Campos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and is established knowledge.

claim: Recombination may be mutagenic and increase diversity, for example via mismatch repair enzymes showing a mutational bias for A:T > G:C transversions.
source: Recombination may also be mutagenic and increase diversity, for example via mismatch repair enzymes showing a mutational bias for A:T > G:C transversions (Duret and Galtier, 2009; Webster and Hurst, 2012; Glémin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The 5 intervals tested range from 0.67–5.40 megabases and represent 11.5% of the genome.
source: The 5 intervals tested (I1b, I1fg, I2f, 420 and CEN3) range from 0.67–5.40 megabases (Mb), represent 11.5% of the genome (14.34 Mb) in total and are located in sub-telomeric, interstitial and centromeric regions (Figure 1A and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 2 and Figure 1A.

claim: The centromeric interval CEN3 has the lowest experimental recombination rate at 2.11 cM/Mb.
source: The intervals vary in experimental recombination rate, with the centromeric interval CEN3 being the lowest (2.11 cM/Mb) and the sub-telomeric interval I2f being the highest (13.02 cM/Mb) (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 2.

claim: The sub-telomeric interval I2f has the highest experimental recombination rate at 13.02 cM/Mb.
source: The intervals vary in experimental recombination rate, with the centromeric interval CEN3 being the lowest (2.11 cM/Mb) and the sub-telomeric interval I2f being the highest (13.02 cM/Mb) (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 2.

claim: Arabidopsis male meiosis shows elevated sub-telomeric recombination.
source: As Arabidopsis male meiosis shows elevated sub-telomeric recombination, this likely contributes to the high I2f crossover frequency, which is measured in pollen (Giraut et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CEN3 shows the highest heterozygosity levels among the intervals tested.
source: To asses relative heterozygosity levels we analysed pairwise sequence differences relative to Col-0 using the 19 genomes dataset, which was generated from a subset of the accessions used in our crosses (Gan et al., 2011). CEN3 shows the highest heterozygosity levels, followed by the interstitial and sub-telomeric intervals (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 2 and citation to the 19 genomes dataset.

claim: CellProfiler image analysis software can be adapted to rapidly score fluorescent seed for crossover measurement.
source: To increase throughput when measuring fluorescent seed we adapted CellProfiler image analysis software, allowing us to rapidly score ∼2000 seed per individual (Figure 2A–F) (Carpenter et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the description of the method and Figure 2.

claim: The CellProfiler method gives recombination measurements not significantly different from manually collected data.
source: This method gives recombination measurements not significantly different from manually collected data (Figure 2F, Figure 2—source data 1) (generalized linear model (GLM), hereafter GLM, p = 0.373).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: 13,264,943 gametes were scored in total across all F1 crosses.
source: Replicate heterozygous F1 individuals were analysed for each cross and 13,264,943 gametes were scored in total, to provide an extensive survey of the influence of polymorphism heterozygosity on crossover frequency (Figure 3 and Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the total number of gametes scored.

claim: F1 heterozygotes showed both significantly higher and lower total recombination compared to Col homozygotes.
source: F1 heterozygotes showed both significantly higher and lower total recombination compared to Col homozygotes (Figure 3 and Table 3) (GLM with 113° of freedom p < 2.0 × 10−16).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 3 and Table 3.

claim: F1 genetic distances and polymorphism levels within the intervals were poorly correlated.
source: F1 genetic distances and polymorphism levels within the intervals were poorly correlated, consistent with previous observations (Table 4) (Barth et al., 2001; Gan et al., 2011; Salomé et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 4 and citations to previous work.

claim: The Shahdara (Sha) accession has a sub-telomeric inversion (3–5.1 Mb) on chromosome 3 relative to Col.
source: For example, the Shahdara (Sha) accession has a sub-telomeric inversion (3–5.1 Mb) on chromosome 3 relative to Col (Loudet et al., 2002; Simon et al., 2008; Salomé et al., 2012), and Col/Sha F1s show consistently low crossovers in 420, which overlaps the inversion (Figure 3D and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Col/Sha F1s show consistently low crossovers in 420, which overlaps the inversion.
source: For example, the Shahdara (Sha) accession has a sub-telomeric inversion (3–5.1 Mb) on chromosome 3 relative to Col (Loudet et al., 2002; Simon et al., 2008; Salomé et al., 2012), and Col/Sha F1s show consistently low crossovers in 420, which overlaps the inversion (Figure 3D and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3D and Table 3.

claim: 10 of 26 F1s showed significantly higher summed crossover frequency compared with Col homozygotes.
source: 10 of 26 F1s showed significantly higher summed crossover frequency compared with Col homozygotes, consistent with previous reports that recombination can increase in heterozygous backgrounds in Arabidopsis (Barth et al., 2001) (Figure 3F and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3F and Table 3.

claim: The 420/++ Col/Ct F2 population showed significantly greater variation in recombination rates than Col/Col homozygotes.
source: The 420/++ Col/Ct F2 population showed significantly greater variation in recombination rates than Col/Col homozygotes (F-test p = 0.0129) (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: No association was detected between Col/Ct markers on chromosomes 1, 2, 4 or 5 and 420 crossover frequency.
source: We genotyped 51 Col/Ct markers throughout the genome and tested for their association with 420 crossover frequency using QTL analysis. We detected no association using markers on chromosomes 1, 2, 4 or 5 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by QTL analysis presented in Figure 4B.

claim: On chromosome 3, homozygosity (Col/Col or Ct/Ct) outside of 420 was associated with high recombination.
source: However, on chromosome 3 itself homozygosity (Col/Col or Ct/Ct) outside of 420 was associated with high recombination (FDR corrected chi-square test p = 3.29 × 10−31) (Figure 4B,E–F and Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 4B, E-F and Table 5.

claim: The I2f/++ Col/Ct F2 population showed significantly greater variation in recombination rates than Col/Col homozygotes.
source: The I2f/++ Col/Ct F2 population also showed significantly greater variation in recombination rates than Col/Col homozygotes (F-test, p = 0.04) (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: For I2f, the highest recombination F2 quartile showed significantly greater marker homozygosity outside I2f on chromosome 2.
source: We performed QTL analysis for Col/Ct markers on chromosomes 2 and 3 and again observed a significant effect on the same chromosome and no trans effect from chromosome 3. An identical trend to that seen for 420 was observed, with the highest recombination F2 quartile showing significantly greater marker homozygosity (both Col/Col and Ct/Ct) outside I2f on chromosome 2 (FDR corrected chi-square test p = 1.44 × 10−10) (Figure 4C,G–I and Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 4C, G-I and Table 6.

claim: CEN3 F2 recombination rates were significantly more variable than Col/Col homozygotes.
source: As for 420 and I2f, CEN3 F2 recombination rates were significantly more variable than Col/Col homozygotes (F-test p = 0.01268) (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For CEN3, 5 markers in proximity to CEN3 were significantly more homozygous in the hottest compared to the coldest F2 quartile.
source: We genotyped 9 Col/Ct markers on chromosome 3 and observed that 5 markers in proximity to CEN3 were significantly more homozygous in the hottest compared to the coldest F2 quartile (FDR corrected chi-square test p = 1.14 × 10−07) (Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 4D-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 7.

claim: I3b crossover frequency significantly increased in HET-HOM compared to HOM-HOM plants.
source: We observed that I3b crossovers significantly increased in HET-HOM compared to HOM-HOM plants, and there was a reciprocal decrease in I3c crossovers (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 2) (both GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: I3c crossovers reciprocally decreased in HET-HOM compared to HOM-HOM plants.
source: We observed that I3b crossovers significantly increased in HET-HOM compared to HOM-HOM plants, and there was a reciprocal decrease in I3c crossovers (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 2) (both GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: In wild type HOM-HOM, genetic distance in the 420 interval significantly increased in fancm and fancm zip4 mutants compared with wild type.
source: When chromosome 3 is Col/Col homozygous (HOM-HOM) genetic distance in the 420 interval significantly increased in fancm and fancm zip4 mutants compared with wild type (both GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 1), consistent with repair of the majority of DSBs via a non-interfering crossover pathway (Crismani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The CEN3 interval experienced a smaller yet significant increase in genetic distance in fancm and decreased in fancm zip4.
source: However, the CEN3 interval experienced a smaller yet significant increase in genetic distance in fancm and decreased in fancm zip4 (both GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16), indicating that non-interfering crossover repair is less efficient in this region (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: In HET-HET plants, the crossover frequency increases seen in fancm and fancm zip4 were strongly suppressed or eliminated relative to HOM-HOM.
source: We next generated plants that were Col/Ct heterozygous (HET-HET) on chromosome 3 and observed that the previous increase in 420 crossovers was strongly suppressed in fancm and fancm zip4 (GLM p = 1.24 × 10−06 and p < 2.0 × 10−16), whereas wild type Col/Ct were slightly but significantly higher than wild type Col/Col (GLM p = 0.0126) (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A-B.

claim: CEN3 crossovers were significantly suppressed by Col/Ct heterozygosity in fancm and nearly eliminated in fancm zip4 compared to Col/Col.
source: CEN3 crossovers were also significantly suppressed by Col/Ct heterozygosity in fancm and nearly eliminated in fancm zip4 compared to Col/Col (both GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Wild type HET-HOM lines show a significant increase in 420 and a reciprocal decrease in CEN3 crossovers compared to wild type HOM-HOM.
source: As expected, wild type HET-HOM lines show a significant increase in 420 and a reciprocal decrease in CEN3 crossovers compared to wild type HOM-HOM (both GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 6A,C), indicating compensatory changes between the two intervals in the HET-HOM lines.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A, C.

claim: HET-HOM lines in fancm zip4 showed lower 420 crossovers than wild type HOM-HOM, demonstrating that the interfering pathway is required for the heterozygosity-homozygosity juxtaposition effect.
source: HET-HOM lines in fancm zip4 showed lower 420 crossovers than wild type HOM-HOM (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16), which demonstrates that the interfering pathway is required for the heterozygosity-homozygosity juxtaposition effect (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A, C.

claim: HOM-HET lines significantly reduced 420 crossovers compared to wild type HOM-HOM.
source: We also generated HOM-HET lines that were homozygous within 420 and heterozygous outside, which significantly reduced 420 crossovers compared to wild type HOM-HOM as expected (GLM p = 7.60 × 10−11) (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A, D.

claim: HOM-HET lines in fancm and fancm zip4 showed high 420 crossovers comparable to HOM-HOM.
source: HOM-HET lines in fancm and fancm zip4 showed high 420 crossovers comparable to HOM-HOM, as the non-interfering crossover repair active in these backgrounds is efficient in homozygous regions (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 6A, D.

claim: CEN3 genetic distance was strongly suppressed in fancm and fancm zip4 HOM-HET lines compared with HOM-HOM.
source: CEN3 genetic distance was again strongly suppressed in fancm and fancm zip4 HOM-HET lines compared with HOM-HOM (both GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16), consistent with heterozygosity inhibiting non-interfering crossover repair (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 6A, D.

claim: Total chiasmata counts were not significantly different between Col/Col homozygotes, Ct/Ct homozygotes, Col/Ct F1 heterozygotes, and recombinant 420-CEN3 lines.
source: Adjacent chiasmata count categories were combined to give a minimum expected value of five for the purposes of a chi-square test with 8° of freedom. This test gave no significant differences in chiasmata between the genotypes (p = 0.3365) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of chiasmata counts presented in Figure 7.

claim: In wild type, genetic distances did not significantly change between HOM-HOM and HET-HET for I3bc.
source: We first compared I3bc plants that were Col/Col homozygous (HOM-HOM) with Col/Ct heterozygotes (HET-HET). In wild type, genetic distances did not significantly change between HOM-HOM and HET-HET (GLM p = 0.352 and p = 0.666), but crossover interference significantly increased (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8A, B.

claim: Crossover interference significantly increased in wild type HET-HET compared to HOM-HOM for I3bc.
source: We first compared I3bc plants that were Col/Col homozygous (HOM-HOM) with Col/Ct heterozygotes (HET-HET). In wild type, genetic distances did not significantly change between HOM-HOM and HET-HET (GLM p = 0.352 and p = 0.666), but crossover interference significantly increased (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 8A,B, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8A, B.

claim: fancm and fancm zip4 showed a significant reduction and an absence of interference respectively in a HOM-HOM background.
source: Consistent with previous observations, fancm and fancm zip4 showed a significant reduction and an absence of interference respectively, in a HOM-HOM background (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16 and p = 4.94 × 10−16) (Figure 8A, Figure 8—source data 2) (Crismani et al., 2012; Yelina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8A and citations to previous work.

claim: In HET-HET plants, the crossover frequency increases seen in fancm and fancm zip4 were greatly suppressed or eliminated relative to HOM-HOM for I3bc.
source: In HET-HET plants the crossover frequency increases seen in fancm and fancm zip4 were again greatly suppressed, or eliminated, relative to HOM-HOM, as observed previously for 420-CEN3 (GLM both p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8B.

claim: Interference measurements significantly increased in both fancm and fancm zip4 mutants in a HET-HET background compared to HOM-HOM for I3bc.
source: Unexpectedly, interference measurements significantly increased in both fancm and fancm zip4 mutants in a HET-HET background compared to HOM-HOM (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16 and p = 4.94 × 10−16) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8B.

claim: zip4 genetic distances were significantly reduced when comparing HOM-HOM to HET-HET backgrounds for I3bc.
source: Finally, we measured I3bc cM in zip4 mutants alone (HOM-HOM) and observed significantly decreased crossovers compared with wild type HOM-HOM (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 8E, Figure 8—source data 1). Importantly, zip4 genetic distances were further significantly reduced when comparing HOM-HOM to HET-HET backgrounds (GLM p = 1.79 × 10−10 and p = 1.53 × 10−9) (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8E.

claim: Wild type I3b and I3c genetic distances both significantly increase in HET-HOM lines relative to HOM-HOM.
source: As expected, wild type I3b and I3c genetic distances both significantly increase in HET-HOM lines relative to HOM-HOM (GLM both p < 2.0 × 10−16), consistent with our previous 420 experiments, and this was associated with a significant increase in crossover interference (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 8A,C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8A, C.

claim: Col/Ct (HET-HOM) heterozygosity suppressed the crossover increases seen in fancm and fancm zip4 for I3bc.
source: As shown earlier, we observed that Col/Ct (HET-HOM) heterozygosity suppressed the crossover increases seen in fancm and fancm zip4 (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16), with the same significant increases in crossover interference strength (GLM p < 2.0 × 10−16 and p = 4.94 × 10−16) (Figure 8A,C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8A, C.

claim: I3b and I3c genetic distances were significantly decreased in wild type HOM-HET compared with wild type HOM-HOM plants.
source: The reciprocal situation was observed in HOM-HET plants where I3bc was Col/Col homozygous and the rest of the chromosome Col/Ct heterozygous. I3b and I3c genetic distances were significantly decreased in wild type HOM-HET compared with wild type HOM-HOM plants (GLM both p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 8A,D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8A, D.

claim: HOM-HET fancm and fancm zip4 plants showed high crossovers for I3bc.
source: HOM-HET fancm and fancm zip4 plants showed high crossovers, as the non-interfering pathway is efficient in the homozygous I3bc interval (Figure 8A,D).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 8A, D.

claim: HET-HOM zip4 lines showed significantly lower I3b and I3c cM than HOM-HOM zip4.
source: We also generated HET-HOM zip4 lines, which unlike wild type showed significantly lower I3b and I3c cM than HOM-HOM zip4 (GLM both P= p < 2.0 × 10−16) (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 8E.

claim: Genetic distance significantly decreased in Col/Ler for six of the eight intervals measured compared to Col/Col.
source: Compared to Col/Col, genetic distance significantly decreased in Col/Ler for six of the eight intervals measured and the remaining two intervals were not significantly changed (Table 8).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 8.

claim: Significant positive interference was detected in all tetrad FTL intervals analyzed.
source: To calculate interference strength we compared cM values in each interval from tetrads that had a crossover in the adjacent interval, to the same intervals in tetrads lacking a crossover in the adjacent interval, and detected significant positive interference in all cases (Table 9) (Berchowitz and Copenhaver, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 9.

claim: Interference strength significantly increased in Col/Ler compared to Col/Col using Fisher's combined probability test.
source: The resulting interference ratios were then compared between Col/Col and Col/Ler using Fisher's combined probability test, which revealed a significant increase in interference strength in Col/Ler (χ2.001[16] = 39.26) (Table 9).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Table 9.

claim: Mismatched precursors in heterozygous regions may be slowed in maturation and trigger feedback mechanisms that cause further DSBs.
source: Therefore, one possibility is that mismatched precursors in heterozygous regions are slowed in maturation and trigger feedback mechanisms that cause further DSBs, for example via ATM/ATR kinase signalling (Carballo et al., 2008; Lange et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011; Kurzbauer et al., 2012; Garcia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Heterozygous regions would receive more 'late' DSBs, leading to more precursors and a higher chance of receiving a crossover designation event.
source: As a consequence, heterozygous regions would receive more 'late' DSBs, leading to more precursors and a higher chance of receiving a crossover designation event.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the proposed model.

claim: An alternative model is that mismatched precursors are more sensitive to crossover designation.
source: An alternative model is that mismatched precursors are more sensitive to crossover designation and thus heterozygous regions have a higher chance of an interfering crossover, leading to similar effects.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative model proposed by the authors.
